name: Tertullian
status: Church Father. Not counted a saint.

seo.title: Tertullian: famous quotes, misquotes, and why he is not a saint
seo.description: Who Tertullian was, in plain words: the first great Latin theologian, his real sayings and famous misquotes, and why he broke with the Church.

band.lede: The first great theologian to write in Latin, who defended the Christians and then broke with the Church.

picture.alt: An engraving of Tertullian as a bearded man in a turban and robe, holding a written scroll over a desk with an inkpot and quill
picture.credit: Tertullian, an imagined portrait, from André Thevet, Les vrais pourtraits et vies des hommes illustres, 1584. Public domain.

card.line: The first great theologian to write in Latin, who defended the Christians and then broke with the Church.

who: Tertullian grew up a pagan in Carthage, in Roman Africa. He became a Christian about 195. He was the first great theologian to write in Latin, and the first known to call God the Trinity in Latin. He defended Christians under persecution. Later he joined the New Prophecy and broke with the Church. No church counts him a saint.

roles.name: Theologian
roles.line: The first to write theology in Latin

lines: Five more under his name are not his

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 160. Some say 155. At **Carthage** in Roman Africa, today near Tunis in **Tunisia**.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: A pagan, at Carthage. His father was a centurion. He was well schooled, above all in rhetoric and law.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: After 220. The year is not known. *Britannica* says at Carthage, but no early source says where. Jerome heard that he lived to a great old age.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: His Latin name is **Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus**. He signs one of his books Septimius Tertullianus.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: No church counts him a saint. He left the Church for the New Prophecy, also called Montanism.

facts.label: Feast day
facts.text: None. No Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Episcopal or Lutheran calendar keeps one for him.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: No likeness from his own time is known. Later engravers imagined him: as a writer in a turban in 1584, or as a bald old man with a long beard.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Thirty-one works survive, all in Latin. At least twelve more are lost, some of them written in Greek. The longest is **Against Marcion**, in five books.

portrait.alt: A French engraving of Tertullian as an old man with a long white beard and a fur-collared cloak, inside an ornate frame, with a French caption below
portrait.credit: Tertullien, an engraving published by Henri Bonnart, Paris, undated. KU Leuven. Public domain.
portrait.caption: A French engraving published by Henri Bonnart, undated. The French line says he was a pagan of Carthage whom God enlightened, and that his books hold as many maxims as words. No true likeness of him survives, so this face is imagined, like the one above. KU Leuven. Public domain.

traits.title: a mocking wit
traits.text: Some ideas, he held, deserve laughter more than an answer. “Even the truth may indulge in ridicule, because it is jubilant.” He asked what Pontic mouse ever gnawed as hard as Marcion, the man “who has gnawed the Gospels to pieces”.

cite.text: Against the Valentinians, chapter 6; Against Marcion, Book 1, chapter 1

traits.title: impatient, and said so
traits.text: He wrote a whole book on patience. In its first chapter he admits he has none. He is “ever sick with the heats of impatience”, he says, and pleads for “that health of patience which I possess not”.

traits.title: tender at home
traits.text: The same man wrote to his own wife about the happiness of a marriage shared in faith. Of such a husband and wife he says: “Together they pray, together prostrate themselves, together perform their fasts; mutually teaching, mutually exhorting, mutually sustaining.”

traits.title: not ashamed to change
traits.text: He knew his critics would call him fickle for leaving his old, milder views. He was glad to have changed: “No one blushes at his own improvement.” And he was proud to stand with the few, since “it is in the company of the few that truth is loved!”

said.lede: No one wrote a *Life* of him. Beyond his own books, we have one short sketch by Jerome. Later writers admired his genius and grieved over his break.

quotes.q: …Cyprian was accustomed never to pass a day without reading Tertullian, and that he frequently said to him, “Give me the master,” meaning by this, Tertullian.
quotes.who: Jerome. He heard it from an old man who had been Cyprian's secretary.

quotes.q: Every word almost was a sentence; every sentence a victory.
quotes.who: Vincent of Lérins, on his style. He ranks him first among the Latin writers, as Origen was among the Greeks.

quotes.q: Can anything be more learned or more pointed than the style of Tertullian? His Apology and his books Against the Gentiles contain all the wisdom of the world.
quotes.who: Jerome, in a letter to Magnus

moments.title: A pagan who laughed
moments.text: He grew up a pagan in Carthage, well schooled in rhetoric and law. He shared the pagan prejudice against the Christians. Years later he told the pagans: “Once these things were with us, too, the theme of ridicule. We are of your stock and nature: men are made, not born, Christians.”

moments.title: The *Apology*
moments.text: Christians were being tried and killed for the name alone. He wrote to the Roman governors to defend them. He answered the rumours about them one by one. He ended with a warning: killing Christians only makes more of them.

moments.title: To the martyrs in prison
moments.text: He wrote a short letter to Christians in prison, waiting to die. He told them to think of it as a retreat: “Let us drop the name of prison; let us call it a place of retirement.”

moments.title: The New Prophecy
moments.text: He came to believe that the Holy Spirit spoke through three prophets from Phrygia: Montanus, Prisca and Maximilla. In his own church a woman had visions during Sunday worship, and he trusted them. Rome turned against the prophets, and he and his friends broke with the rest of the Church. He began to call other Christians {la|Psychici}, the unspiritual. In his own words: “We indeed, on our part, subsequently withdrew from the carnally-minded on our acknowledgment and maintenance of the Paraclete.”

cite.text: Against Praxeas, chapter 1; On the Soul, chapter 9; Catholic Encyclopedia

moments.title: The soldier's crown
moments.text: The emperors gave the army a bonus, and the soldiers came up wearing laurel crowns. One carried his in his hand. Asked why, he said, “I am a Christian.” He put down his cloak, his boots and his sword, and went to prison. Then people began to call him headstrong and rash, and too eager to die. Tertullian says he cannot tell whether they were Christians, since the pagans said the same. He wrote a book to defend the soldier. Of the Christians who shrank from martyrdom he wrote: “their pastors are lions in peace, deer in the fight.”

moments.title: A warning to the governor
moments.text: Scapula, the governor of Africa, was persecuting Christians. Tertullian wrote to warn him. No one should be forced into a religion: “It is assuredly no part of religion to compel religion.” He reminded Scapula what Christians had done for emperors. Severus kept in his palace a Christian who had once cured him by anointing. And in a famous thirst, the army of Marcus Aurelius got rain “by the prayers his Christian soldiers offered to God”.

moments.title: A group of his own
moments.text: In time he parted from the Montanists as well, and led his own followers, the Tertullianists. Jerome heard that he lived to a great old age. His group lasted about two hundred years. In Augustine's day its last few members joined the Catholic Church, and handed over their church building.

cite.text: Jerome, Illustrious Men, chapter 53; Augustine, On Heresies, chapter 86; New Catholic Encyclopedia

words.note: His surviving books are in Latin. These lines are from the *Ante-Nicene Fathers*, in the translations of S. Thelwall and Peter Holmes (American edition, 1885).

feature.q: The oftener we are mown down by you, the more in number we grow; the blood of Christians is seed.
feature.ctx: The last chapter of the *Apology*. The saying about the blood of the martyrs comes from here. In Latin, {la|Plures efficimur, quotiens metimur a vobis: semen est sanguis Christianorum.}

quotes.q: What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord is there between the Academy and the Church? what between heretics and Christians?
quotes.who: Against mixing philosophy into the faith. He blamed the philosophers for the heresies. In Latin, {la|Quid ergo Athenis et Hierosolymis?}

quotes.q: O noble testimony of the soul by nature Christian!
quotes.who: On the pagans' everyday cries, such as “God sees”. The soul itself, he says, knows God. In Latin, {la|O testimonium animae naturaliter Christianae!}

quotes.q: We are but of yesterday, and we have filled every place among you
quotes.who: On how fast the Church had grown. The temples of the gods, he says, are all that is left to them.

quotes.q: It is peculiar to Christians alone to love those that hate them.
quotes.who: To the governor who was persecuting them.

quotes.q: The leg does not feel the chain when the mind is in the heavens.
quotes.who: To Christians in prison, waiting to die.

quotes.q: If I should offer you a rose, you will not disdain its Maker.
quotes.who: To Marcion, who scorned the Maker of the world.

quotes.q: Prayer is alone that which vanquishes God.
quotes.who: On the power of prayer. In the same chapter, birds rising in flight “expand the cross of their wings”.

quotes.q: Only, I pray that, when you are asking, you be mindful likewise of Tertullian the sinner.
quotes.who: The last words of his book *On Baptism*. He asks the newly baptized to remember him when they first pray.

extras.title: His hardest words
extras.lede: He could be very harsh, and his critics have long said so. Here are the lines they point to, in his own words, beside what they say.

items.title: No pardon for adultery
items.text: A bishop announced that adultery would be forgiven after penance. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* thinks it was probably Pope Callistus. Tertullian mocked him as “the bishop of bishops”. The Church could forgive such sins, he said, but should not. He gave the words to the Paraclete, speaking through the new prophets. Years before, in On Repentance, he had allowed one more repentance after baptism. Baptism shuts the gate of forgiveness, he wrote then, but God “has permitted it still to stand somewhat open”.
items.quote: The Church has the power to forgive sins; but I will not do it, lest they commit others withal.

cite.text: On Modesty, chapters 1 and 21; On Repentance, chapter 7

items.title: Joy at the Judgment
items.text: The Shows warns Christians away from the games. It ends with a greater show to come: the Last Judgment. Rulers once declared gods groan in the darkness, and governors who persecuted Christians burn in the fire. His critics have long held lines like this against him. In Gibbon's verdict, the *New Catholic Encyclopedia* notes, he is little better than a sadist. The same article calls such verdicts exaggerations.
items.quote: How vast a spectacle then bursts upon the eye! What there excites my admiration? what my derision? Which sight gives me joy? which rouses me to exultation?

items.title: On women
items.text: In a book urging Christian women to dress plainly, he tells each of them she is an Eve, and still bears Eve's guilt. In *On Baptism* he says a woman may not teach or baptize. Yet he trusted a woman prophet in his own church, and praised “the most heroic martyr Perpetua”.
items.quote: You are the devil's gateway: you are the unsealer of that (forbidden) tree: you are the first deserter of the divine law

cite.text: On the Apparel of Women, Book 1, chapter 1; On Baptism, chapter 17

items.title: No running from persecution
items.text: In his Montanist years he taught that a Christian must never flee persecution, because God means the suffering. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* calls it “This intolerable doctrine”, and notes he had not held it before.
items.quote: He who fears to suffer, cannot belong to Him who suffered.

cite.text: On Flight in Persecution, chapter 14; Catholic Encyclopedia

myths.claim: He said “I believe because it is absurd”, in Latin {la|Credo quia absurdum}.
myths.truth: Not in those words. Arguing against Marcion that Christ's flesh was real, he wrote of His death: “it is by all means to be believed, because it is absurd.” The Latin word is {la|ineptum}, foolish, not {la|absurdum}. Peter Harrison finds the “I believe” form first in Voltaire, in 1767, who gave it to Augustine.

cite.text: On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 5; Peter Harrison, Church History, 2017

myths.claim: He wrote, “The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church.”
myths.truth: A later smoothing. He wrote “the blood of Christians is seed”. The words martyrs and Church are not in it.

myths.claim: The pagans praised the Christians: “See how they love one another!”
myths.truth: He does report pagans saying it. Such love, he says, leads many “to put a brand upon us”. And he adds why it struck them: they themselves hated one another. “See, they say, how they love one another, for themselves are animated by mutual hatred”.
He is not a saint. The *Roman Martyrology* does keep a St Tertullian, on 27 April. That is another man, a bishop of Bologna.

myths.claim: He was a priest of Carthage.
myths.truth: Only Jerome says so. In his own books he writes as a layman: “Are not even we laics priests?” The *Catholic Encyclopedia* says he became a priest. The Encyclopedia of Religion says he was never ordained.

cite.text: On Exhortation to Chastity, chapter 7; Jerome, Illustrious Men, chapter 53

myths.claim: He was a Roman lawyer, the jurist Tertullianus quoted in the Roman law books.
myths.truth: Possible, not proven. Eusebius calls him “a man well versed in the laws of the Romans”. On the jurist, the reference books disagree. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* doubts it. The *New Catholic Encyclopedia* accepts it. The Encyclopedia of Religion rejects it.
He is the first known writer to use it in Latin, {la|trinitas}. But Theophilus of Antioch had already used the Greek word. He writes of “the Trinity, of God, and His Word, and His wisdom”.

cite.text: New Catholic Encyclopedia; Theophilus, To Autolycus, Book 2, chapter 15

myths.claim: He came back to the Church before he died.
myths.truth: No ancient source says so. The *New Catholic Encyclopedia* finds no evidence that he did.

stood.lede: Each line is his own, in the *Ante-Nicene Fathers* translation. The free copies online misprint one word in the war line. So its link goes to the printed book of 1869, which reads “unbelted”.

circle.name: His wife
circle.text: He wrote her two books. He asked her not to marry again after his death. If she did, she should marry only a Christian. Her name is not recorded.

circle.name: Cyprian of Carthage
circle.text: Bishop of Carthage a generation later. He read Tertullian every day and called him “the master”. But, says Jerome, he did not follow him into the New Prophecy.

circle.name: Perpetua
circle.text: A martyr of Carthage. He calls her “the most heroic martyr Perpetua”, and cites her vision of Paradise.

circle.name: Irenaeus of Lyons
circle.text: He names Irenaeus among the writers he wished to follow closely: “Irenæus, that very exact inquirer into all doctrines”.

circle.name: Marcion
circle.text: His great opponent. Tertullian wrote five books against the man who rejected the God of the Old Testament and cut down the Gospels.

circle.name: Praxeas
circle.text: A teacher who brought to Rome the idea that the Father Himself was born and suffered. Tertullian says he also turned the bishop of Rome against the new prophets: “he put to flight the Paraclete, and he crucified the Father.”

circle.name: Hermogenes
circle.text: A painter who taught that matter had always existed alongside God. Tertullian wrote a book against him, and says he “mistakes loquacity for eloquence”.

saint.big: No. No church counts him a saint. He left the Church for the New Prophecy, and later led a group of his own.

churches.note: Not in the calendar or the *Roman Martyrology*
A great church writer, but not a Father
Not in the Church of England or Episcopal calendars
Not in the Missouri Synod or ELCA calendars

paras: Jerome says he went over to Montanus “driven by the envy and abuse of the clergy of the Roman church”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* doubts that he left by his own act. When Rome rejected the prophets, it says, the Church of Carthage put out at least the most violent of their followers.

Augustine counts him a heretic. Not for teaching that the soul and even God are bodies, he says. It was for going over to the Montanists he had once attacked, and for condemning second marriages as fornication.
A later list of books to receive and to reject, the Gelasian Decree, names his works among the books the Church does not receive.

Is he a Church Father? Many call him one, and the *Ante-Nicene Fathers* series prints his books. But the *New Catholic Encyclopedia* says he cannot be given a place among the Fathers. The Russian Orthodox site azbyka.ru calls him an outstanding church writer, but not a Father of the Church, because he fell away.

quotes.q: In the case of Tertullian we praise his great talent, but we condemn his heresy.
…this Tertullian, I say, too little tenacious of Catholic doctrine, that is, of the universal and ancient faith, more eloquent by far than faithful, changed his belief.

reads.text: His defence of the Christians, written to the Roman governors in 197. This is where “the blood of Christians is seed” comes from.

tidbits.text: Christians in his day traced the cross on their foreheads at every turn: going out, coming in, dressing, bathing, at table. No Scripture commands it, he says. Tradition began it, and custom kept it.

Christians were blamed for every disaster. If the Tiber flooded or the Nile did not, if the rain failed or the earth shook, the crowd cried for the Christians to be thrown to the lion. Could one beast eat so many? he asked.
A man paid to dodge beasts in the arena paraded a picture of the God of the Christians, with donkey's ears and one hoof, holding a book and wearing a toga. The Christians laughed, he says.
Carthage mocked him for swapping the toga for a philosopher's cloak, so he wrote a witty book in its defence. The toga needs its folds set the day before, he says. The cloak goes on in one throw.

cite.text: On the Pallium, chapters 1 and 5; Catholic Encyclopedia
